title: Understanding Digital Signal Processing, Third Edition
topics: Front matter (PDF pp. 1-25): preface, intended audience, third-edition changes, acknowledgments, notation, and contents for the assigned material.
1.1 Discrete Sequences and Systems (PDF p. 26): sampled sequences, sample indices, amplitude, and the fact that a discrete sequence has no defined values between samples.
1.2 Signal Amplitude, Magnitude, Power (PDF p. 32): signed amplitude, nonnegative magnitude, and power proportional to squared amplitude.
1.3 Signal Processing Operational Symbols (PDF p. 33): adders, multipliers, and unit delays as the primitives of DSP block diagrams.
1.4 Introduction to Discrete Linear Time-Invariant Systems (PDF p. 35): linearity, additivity, homogeneity, and time invariance.

1.8 Analyzing Linear Time-Invariant Systems (PDF p. 42): impulse response, convolution, and frequency response.

key_results: Sec. 1.1 (PDF pp. 26-32): a discrete sequence is defined only at integer sample indices; absolute frequency requires the sample period or sample rate, not merely the plotted sample pattern.

Secs. 1.4-1.6 (PDF pp. 35-41): LTI status requires both superposition (additivity plus homogeneity) and invariance to a time shift; squaring is a memorable counterexample because it creates DC, harmonics, and intermodulation products.

Secs. 1.7-1.8 (PDF pp. 41-43): cascaded LTI systems commute, and an LTI system is completely characterized by its impulse response; output is input convolved with that response, while its transform is the system frequency response.
Sec. 2.1 (PDF pp. 52-55): samples of a sinusoid at f0 are indistinguishable from sinusoids at f0+kfs; sampling therefore replicates the continuous spectrum at integer multiples of fs.

Sec. 2.2 (PDF pp. 56-59): a baseband signal limited to B Hz needs fs >= 2B, but the practical acquisition chain still needs an analog lowpass anti-alias filter because any energy above fs/2 folds irreversibly into baseband.

Sec. 2.3 (PDF pp. 59-63): a bandpass signal can often be sampled below twice its highest frequency when its occupied bandwidth is narrow; permissible sample-rate intervals depend on center frequency, bandwidth, and an integer spectral-zone index, while fs must remain at least 2B.
Sec. 2.4 (PDF pp. 63-65): odd spectral folding reverses a band; multiplying samples by (-1)^n shifts the spectrum by fs/2 and can restore its orientation.

Sec. 2.4 (PDF pp. 64-65): bandpass sampling folds out-of-band noise into the recovered band; for the text's zone index m, noise power grows by approximately m+1 and the SNR penalty is 10 log10(m+1) dB (3 dB at m=1).

Sec. 3.1 (PDF pp. 75-85): the N-point DFT measures correlation with complex sinusoids containing integer cycle counts over the N-sample record; bin spacing is Delta f=fs/N, and X(0) is N times the sequence mean.

Sec. 3.2 (PDF pp. 86-87): for real x(n), X(N-m)=X*(m), so an even-length DFT has only N/2+1 independent bins; real-even inputs transform to real-even spectra and real-odd inputs to imaginary-odd spectra.

Sec. 3.4 (PDF p. 88): a bin-centered real sinusoid of peak amplitude A produces magnitude AN/2 in each of its two conjugate bins, a complex sinusoid produces AN in one bin, and DC level D produces DN at bin zero.
Sec. 3.6 (PDF pp. 89-91): circularly shifting the input by k samples multiplies bin m by exp(-j2pi mk/N); magnitude is unchanged and phase acquires a linear ramp.
Sec. 3.7 (PDF pp. 91-92): the IDFT reconstructs the N samples from the bins, reversing the exponent sign and applying the factor 1/N.

Sec. 3.8 (PDF pp. 92-99): a noninteger number of cycles in the record creates an endpoint discontinuity; the finite rectangular observation window makes a tone's spectrum spread according to a sampled sinc/Dirichlet response rather than remain in one bin.
Sec. 3.9 (PDF pp. 99-106): windows reduce leakage sidelobes by tapering endpoints but broaden the main lobe; this is a sensitivity-versus-resolution tradeoff, not a universal improvement.

Secs. 3.9-3.10 (PDF pp. 104-107): the rectangular window's first sidelobe is about -13 dB, and a tone halfway between bins reads only about 0.637 of its true amplitude (roughly 4 dB low in power); Hann/Hanning reduces midpoint scalloping loss to about 1.45 dB while widening the main lobe.

Sec. 3.11 (PDF pp. 107-110): zero padding samples the same DTFT more densely and improves plot/peak interpolation, but it does not resolve tones that the nonzero observation duration cannot separate; acquire about 1/Fres seconds of actual data for resolution Fres.
Sec. 3.12 (PDF pp. 110-113): DFT processing gain for a coherent tone in broadband noise rises by approximately 3 dB whenever N doubles.

Sec. 3.13 (PDF pp. 113-125): a K-sample rectangular pulse has a Dirichlet-kernel spectrum with peak K, first zero near bin N/K, and a main-lobe width of about 2N/K bins, demonstrating the reciprocal time-width/frequency-width relation.

Sec. 3.14 (PDF pp. 125-128): the DTFT is continuous and periodic; an N-point DFT is N uniformly spaced samples of that DTFT and also represents the spectrum of the finite record treated as one period of a periodic sequence.
Sec. 4.1 (PDF pp. 138-140): a radix-2 FFT computes the exact DFT with roughly (N/2)log2(N) complex multiplications instead of N^2; the advantage grows dramatically with N.

Sec. 4.2 (PDF pp. 140-143): choose the nonzero record length from required resolution, pad upward to a convenient FFT length rather than discard valid data, remove mean before applying a window, apply the window before zero padding, and normalize amplitude for real versus complex inputs and window coherent gain.

Sec. 4.3 (PDF pp. 143-150): radix-2 decimation-in-time recursively splits an N-point DFT into even- and odd-index N/2 transforms and joins them with twiddle-factor butterflies; the upper-half outputs reuse lower-half terms with a sign change.
Secs. 4.4-4.5 (PDF pp. 150-154): bit reversal follows from recursive index partitioning; an optimized radix-2 butterfly needs one complex multiplication and two complex additions.

Sec. 4.6 (PDF pp. 154-157): in-place FFTs reduce working storage to about 2N real words but require more intricate addressing, whereas alternating input/output buffers use about 4N real words and simplify routing; twiddles can be precomputed.

Secs. 5.1-5.2 (PDF pp. 168-181): an M-tap FIR output is the convolution sum of current and delayed input samples with M coefficients, and those coefficients are exactly the filter impulse response; the response ends after M output intervals once a finite input ends.

Secs. 5.2-5.3 (PDF pp. 171-195): time-domain convolution corresponds to frequency-domain multiplication, so a filter response is the transform of its impulse response; inverse-transforming an ideal brick-wall response gives an infinite sinc-like impulse response that must be truncated for implementation.

Sec. 5.3 (PDF pp. 181-195): increasing rectangularly truncated FIR length narrows the transition but does not eliminate Gibbs ripple amplitude; a tapered window lowers sidelobe/ripple levels at the cost of a broader transition.

Secs. 5.4-5.5 (PDF pp. 195-197): multiplying lowpass coefficients by a cosine translates the response to bandpass; the fs/4 case yields many zero products, and multiplying coefficient k by (-1)^k translates a lowpass response by fs/2 to make a highpass filter.

Sec. 5.6 (PDF pp. 197-200): Parks-McClellan exchange design finds a Chebyshev-optimal equiripple FIR approximation and normally achieves a narrower transition than a same-length window-designed filter for comparable ripple constraints.

Sec. 5.7 (PDF pp. 200-201): an odd-tap half-band lowpass has symmetry about fs/4 and alternating zero coefficients except its center tap; a 31-tap example needs only 17 multiplications rather than 31.

Sec. 5.8 (PDF pp. 201-206): symmetric or antisymmetric FIR coefficients produce linear phase and constant group delay (N-1)/2 samples; even-tap filters can therefore realize half-sample delay, and linear phase prevents waveform dispersion within the passband.
Sec. 5.9 (PDF pp. 206-216): convolution of finite sequences of lengths P and Q has length P+Q-1; the graphical algorithm reverses one sequence, shifts it, multiplies overlapping samples, and sums.

Sec. 5.10 (PDF pp. 216-224): FIR response can be evaluated directly as a DTFT or with a sufficiently zero-padded FFT of the coefficients; DC gain equals the coefficient sum, phase slope gives group delay, and tap count grows with stopband attenuation and shrinks with transition width.

Secs. 6.1-6.4 (PDF pp. 238-262): an IIR filter adds previous outputs to its difference equation; replacing a one-sample delay by z^-1 turns the block diagram into H(z), and substituting z=exp(jomega) gives its complex frequency response.

Sec. 6.2 (PDF pp. 240-251): on the Laplace s-plane, a stable causal continuous system has every pole in the left half-plane; real part sets exponential growth/decay and imaginary part sets oscillation frequency, while H(jomega) is the frequency response.

Sec. 6.3 (PDF pp. 251-254): the z-plane unit circle is the discrete-frequency contour from -pi to pi radians/sample; a causal IIR filter is stable only if all poles lie inside it, and pole angle sets resonant/oscillation frequency.

Sec. 6.4 (PDF pp. 254-262): a worked second-order IIR has a steeper, lower-sidelobe magnitude response than a five-tap FIR at the same five-multiply workload, but it has nonlinear phase and an asymmetrical, theoretically infinite impulse response.

Sec. 6.5 (PDF pp. 262-267): poles raise response near their unit-circle angles and zeros suppress it; proximity to the unit circle strengthens the effect, a pole or zero on the circle yields infinite gain or attenuation, coincident pairs cancel, and origin poles/zeros do not change frequency response.

Sec. 6.6 (PDF pp. 267-270): Direct Forms I and II and transposed Direct Form II are algebraically equivalent at infinite precision; Direct Form II halves delay storage, while Direct Form I generally resists coefficient/stability error best and transposed Direct Form II behaves better than ordinary Direct Form II in fixed point.

Sec. 6.7 (PDF pp. 270-272): finite word length shifts poles/zeros, permits overflow, and can create zero-input limit cycles through correlated rounding; mitigations include wider words, scaling, saturation arithmetic, dither (with SNR cost), floating point, or an FIR when feedback is unacceptable.

Sec. 6.8 (PDF pp. 272-276): cascaded transfer functions and responses multiply and their impulse responses convolve; parallel transfer functions/responses and impulse responses add. For small linear passband ripples, cascaded ripple is approximately the sum of the section ripples.

Sec. 6.8.2 (PDF pp. 274-276): high-order IIR filters are usually factored into cascaded biquads because low-order sections are easier to scale and less sensitive to coefficient quantization; pair nearby poles and zeros, then order sections by pole distance from the unit circle.

Sec. 6.9 (PDF pp. 276-278): IIR DC gain is the feedforward-coefficient sum divided by one minus the feedback-coefficient sum; scaling feedforward paths can normalize gain without changing response shape, while internal scaling controls overflow/SNR.

Sec. 6.10 (PDF pp. 278-292): impulse invariance samples an analog prototype's impulse response and maps analog poles into the z-plane, but replicated responses alias; it is most suitable for narrow lowpass designs with cutoff far below fs and should not be used for highpass design.

Sec. 6.10 (PDF pp. 280-291): two impulse-invariance workflows are given: inverse-Laplace then z-transform, or partial-fraction decomposition followed by single-pole mappings; including the sample-period factor preserves prototype gain.

Sec. 6.11 (PDF pp. 292-302): the bilinear substitution s=(2/ts)(1-z^-1)/(1+z^-1) maps the left s half-plane inside the unit circle and maps the entire jomega axis one-to-one around the unit circle, avoiding response aliasing.

Sec. 6.11 (PDF pp. 294-301): bilinear frequency mapping is nonlinear: digital frequency approaches pi as analog frequency tends to infinity; prewarp critical analog cutoff frequencies to land them at the desired digital frequencies.

Sec. 6.11.1 (PDF pp. 298-302): in the worked second-order Chebyshev example, bilinear design gives a sharper aliased-free rolloff but uses five multiplications per output versus three for the impulse-invariance implementation; neither method can repair aliasing already present in sampled input data.

Sec. 6.12 (PDF pp. 302-303): optimized IIR design iteratively adjusts numerator and denominator coefficients to minimize a specified response error and is the practical default for arbitrary shapes and often for standard filters as well.

Sec. 6.13 (PDF pp. 303-305): FIR is required for exact linear phase, while IIR often meets magnitude requirements with fewer multipliers and can emulate analog prototypes; on a real DSP, benchmark both because FIR MAC loops can outperform multiply-count intuition.

An ideal discrete-time differentiator has H(ω)=jω: magnitude proportional to |ω| and a +90° phase shift for positive frequency. First- and central-difference FIR approximations trade usable linear bandwidth, high-frequency noise gain, and delay; an antisymmetric length-(D+1) FIR differentiator has group delay D/2. [§7.1.1, Eqs. 7-2–7-7, Figs. 7-1–7-3]

Windowed narrowband differentiators (Hamming, Lanczos, and super-Lanczos variants) reduce high-frequency noise at the cost of a narrower accurate differentiation band and more multiplies. [§7.1.2, Fig. 7-4]

The wideband differentiator impulse response follows from the inverse Fourier transform of the ideal response; the practical coefficient expression in Eq. 7-15 supports arbitrary cutoff, odd or even tap counts, and nonnegative coefficient indexing. Parks–McClellan optimization becomes attractive for longer filters, while even-tap designs impose fractional-sample delay. [§§7.1.3–7.1.4, Eqs. 7-8–7-15]

Rectangular-, trapezoidal-, Simpson-, and Tick-rule digital integrators approximate the ideal 1/|ω| magnitude and −90° phase. Simpson and Tick are most accurate at low frequency, but their z=−1 poles amplify Nyquist-region noise; every listed integrator has a z=1 pole and therefore needs enough word width to tolerate accumulated DC bias. [§§7.2.1–7.2.5, Figs. 7-6–7-10]

For a known finite signal in additive white Gaussian noise, a matched filter maximizes output SNR. Its frequency response is the conjugated signal spectrum with a delay, and its N-sample digital impulse response is the time-reversed signal h(k)=x_s(N−1−k); consequently matched filtering is correlation. [§7.3.1, Eqs. 7-28–7-34]

Matched-filter detection requires a threshold: raising it reduces false alarms but increases missed detections. Direct convolution is natural for short templates, while FFT convolution may be more efficient once the template is roughly longer than 80 samples. [§§7.3.2–7.3.3, Figs. 7-12–7-13]

An interpolated FIR (IFIR) design expands a sparse model filter by replacing each unit delay with M delays, which compresses and repeats its frequency response; a shorter image-reject filter then removes the unwanted replicas. The expansion factor is chosen to minimize the combined model-plus-image-reject tap count subject to transition constraints. [§§7.4.1–7.4.3, Figs. 7-14–7-17]

IFIR efficiency depends on preserving the two sparse stages rather than convolving them into one ordinary FIR. Efficient implementations exploit stride-M addressing and folded linear-phase structures; the architecture trades extra state memory for far fewer multiplications. [§§7.4.4–7.4.5]

A frequency-sampling filter (FSF) cascades a comb, whose zeros are the Nth roots of unity, with resonators that cancel selected comb zeros. When only a few DFT frequency samples are nonzero, this realizes a narrowband FIR filter with far less arithmetic than a direct-form implementation. [§§7.5.1–7.5.2, Figs. 7-23–7-29]

Finite coefficient precision can push nominal unit-circle resonator poles outside the unit circle. Moving poles and matching zeros to radius r<1 guarantees stability; a fixed-point-friendly choice is r=1−2^(−B), chosen as close to one as the word format permits. [§7.5.3, Figs. 7-30–7-32]

The Type-IV real-valued FSF is the preferred architecture in this treatment: it is guaranteed stable, uses real coefficients, has highly linear phase, supports highpass designs, and admits transition-band coefficients that materially improve ripple and stopband attenuation. [§§7.5.4–7.5.10]

The source’s design boundary is empirical: Type-IV FSFs are often more efficient than Parks–McClellan FIR filters when the passband is below about f_s/5 and the transition width is below about f_s/8. [§§7.5.11–7.5.15, Fig. 7-48]

A quadrature signal is a two-dimensional complex signal with mutually orthogonal in-phase and quadrature components. Multiplication by j rotates a complex sample 90° counterclockwise and multiplication by −j rotates it clockwise. [§§8.1–8.2, Figs. 8-1–8-4]

Euler’s identity represents a real cosine or sine as the sum or difference of oppositely rotating complex exponentials. This phasor representation supplies the link between time-domain sinusoids, complex-plane rotation, and spectral impulses. [§8.3, Eqs. 8-7–8-14, Figs. 8-5–8-11]

Negative frequency denotes clockwise complex-plane rotation under the book’s convention. Real signals have conjugate-symmetric spectra, whereas an analytic complex signal can contain only positive-frequency content. [§§8.4–8.6, Figs. 8-12–8-15]

Complex multiplication by exp(+j2πf_ot) shifts a spectrum upward by f_o; the negative-exponent mixer shifts it downward. The spectral-circle view makes alias wraparound at ±f_s/2 explicit. [§§8.6–8.7, Figs. 8-16–8-20]

Quadrature down-conversion uses coherent cosine and sine mixers to form I and Q baseband sequences. Compared with a single real high-rate path it can halve the required converter rate, reduce power, widen processable bandwidth, and make instantaneous magnitude and phase directly available. [§8.8, Figs. 8-18–8-21]

Digitizing before quadrature mixing removes one A/D converter and avoids analog I/Q phase mismatch. At f_c=f_s/4 the oscillator sequences contain only 0 and ±1, so the mixer needs no general multipliers. [§8.9, Figs. 8-22–8-24]
The Hilbert transform applies −j to positive frequencies and +j to negative frequencies, producing a 90° phase shift without changing magnitude. [§9.1, Figs. 9-2–9-3]

The analytic signal x_c=x_r+jH{x_r} cancels the negative-frequency half of a real signal’s spectrum and doubles its positive-frequency half. Its magnitude, angle, and angle derivative provide envelope, instantaneous phase, and instantaneous frequency. [§9.2, Figs. 9-4–9-8]
The ideal discrete Hilbert-transform impulse response is odd and antisymmetric, is zero at even indices, and decays at odd indices as 1, 1/3, 1/5, …. [§9.3, Fig. 9-9]

Odd-tap Type-III FIR Hilbert transformers have zeros at DC and Nyquist and integer group delay; even-tap Type-IV designs retain Nyquist response but require fractional-sample delay. Windowing the truncated ideal impulse response reduces Gibbs ripple while narrowing the useful band. [§9.4.1, Figs. 9-10–9-13]

A time-domain analytic-signal generator must delay the real path by the Hilbert FIR group delay before pairing it with the quadrature output. Antisymmetric coefficient conventions also require attention to coefficient reversal in convolution. [§9.4.1, Fig. 9-12]

For even-length blocks, an FFT-domain analytic-signal construction doubles positive-frequency bins, zeros negative-frequency bins, leaves DC and the Nyquist endpoint with their required half weighting, and inverse-transforms. It is often the best high-performance block method and avoids a separate path-alignment delay. [§9.4.2, Fig. 9-14]

A complex bandpass FIR can generate I/Q outputs with useful filtering, but its real output need not equal the original input; the standard Hilbert pair preserves the input but adds no band selection. The DFT method is the full-band block-processing alternative. [§§9.5–9.6, Figs. 9-15–9-17]

Decimation by M is anti-alias lowpass filtering followed by retaining every Mth sample, giving f_s,new=f_s,old/M. Implementations should avoid computing outputs that will be discarded. [§10.1, Figs. 10-1–10-3]

Two-stage decimation M=M_1M_2 can reduce the total filter order dramatically, typically placing the larger factor first. In the 400 kHz-to-4 kHz, 60 dB example, a single-stage estimate is 2727 taps, whereas near-optimal M_1=25 and M_2=4 requires only a few hundred. [§§10.2.1–10.2.3, Fig. 10-4]

Downsampling is not time invariant. It leaves retained sample amplitudes unchanged, while normalized discrete-frequency spectral magnitudes scale by 1/M and shifted spectral copies can alias. [§§10.3.1–10.3.2, Figs. 10-5–10.8]

Interpolation by L inserts L−1 zeros between input samples and then lowpass filters the resulting images. To preserve constant-signal amplitude, the interpolation filter must have DC gain L. [§§10.4–10.5, Figs. 10-9–10-14]

Rational sample-rate conversion by L/M normally interpolates first, applies one shared lowpass filter, and then decimates, with the passband limited by the smaller input/output Nyquist band. [§§10.6, 10.11, Figs. 10-15 and 10-24]

Polyphase decomposition divides a prototype into subfilters and, using the noble identities, moves filtering to the low-rate side of a sampler. This eliminates multiplies by inserted zeros and computations for discarded outputs; an M-fold decimator reduces multiplication rate by approximately M. [§§10.7, 10.9–10.11, Figs. 10-18–10-24]

Half-band FIR filters have every other coefficient zero except the center coefficient, making them especially efficient for powers-of-two conversion. In cascaded interpolation the later, higher-rate stages can use progressively fewer taps; tiny theoretical zero coefficients should be forced to exact zero in implementation. [§10.12, Figs. 10-25–10-30]

A CIC filter is a cascade of integrators and combs equivalent to repeated moving-average filters. It uses only additions and subtractions, has linear phase and sinc-like magnitude, and is unconditionally stable when its unit coefficients are represented exactly. Its DC gain is D^Q for differential delay D and order Q. [§§10.14.1–10.14.3, Figs. 10-33–10-37]

For CIC decimation, integrators operate before the downsampler and combs after it; interpolation reverses that order, keeping comb computation at the low rate. Two’s-complement internal wraparound is harmless if register widths and the final comb difference satisfy the stated gain bound. [§10.14.4, Figs. 10-38–10-40]

A short FIR compensation filter can approximate the inverse of the CIC passband droop. Compensation should be confined to roughly the first quarter of the first CIC null to avoid excessive high-frequency noise amplification. [§10.14.5, Figs. 10-41–10-43]

Coherent averaging requires sample/phase synchronization and preserves a repeatable signal while uncorrelated zero-mean noise decreases: variance falls as 1/N, standard deviation as 1/√N, and SNR improves by 10log10(N) dB. [§11.1, Eqs. 11-1–11-14, Figs. 11-1–11-3]

Incoherent averaging of magnitude or power spectra reduces display variance and measurement fluctuation, but it does not lower the average noise floor or improve the underlying signal-to-noise ratio. [§11.2, Fig. 11-4]

Averaging several shorter FFT magnitudes can be cheaper and more display-stable than one long transform but sacrifices frequency resolution. Coherent complex-bin averaging is meaningful only when records are synchronized to repeatable periodic content. [§11.3, Figs. 11-5–11-7]
Circular phase data must be averaged as complex vectors, not as scalar angles; angles near +π and −π otherwise average spuriously near zero. [§11.4, Fig. 11-8]

An N-point moving average is an FIR lowpass with sinc-like magnitude and equally spaced unit-circle zeros. Its recursive form produces the same response with two additions per output regardless of N, and white-noise variance is reduced by N. [§11.5, Figs. 11-9–11-11]

The exponential averager y(n)=αx(n)+(1−α)y(n−1) has one pole at z=1−α. Smaller α gives stronger smoothing but slower response; its white-noise variance-reduction factor is (2−α)/α, so α=2/(R+1) targets reduction R and α≈2/(N+1) roughly matches an N-point moving average. [§§11.6.1–11.6.2, Figs. 11-12–11-14]

For a signed fixed-point word with one sign bit and b magnitude bits, dynamic range is approximately 6.02b dB—the familiar 6 dB per bit rule. Binary-point placement trades representable range against resolution without changing the underlying two’s-complement adder or multiplier behavior. [§§12.1.6–12.2, Eq. 12-6]

A b-bit ideal A/D converter with peak range ±V_p has quantization step q=2V_p/2^b. Under the uniform, stationary, signal-uncorrelated error model, quantization error lies in ±q/2 with variance q²/12. [§12.3.1, Eqs. 12-7–12-10, Figs. 12-1–12-3]

Ideal A/D SNR is 6.02b+4.77+20log10(LF) dB for loading factor LF=V_rms/V_p; a full-scale sine gives 6.02b+1.76 dB. Practical design needs headroom and nonideal converters often deliver 3–6 dB less; useful converter SNR should be only about 6 dB above the analog signal’s SNR. [§12.3.1, Eqs. 12-11–12-16, Fig. 12-4]

The sum of m unsigned b-bit values can require b+ceil(log2 m) bits. Two’s-complement additions may wrap at intermediate stages yet still yield the correct final sum when the true final value is representable; overflow is detected when carry into and out of the sign bit differ. [§12.3.2, Fig. 12-5]

FFT butterflies can grow a component by more than a factor of two in one stage, and feedback networks need accumulator width for their DC gain: at least the input width plus ceil(log2 G) bits for gain G. [§12.3.2, Eqs. 12-17–12-22, Fig. 12-6]

Truncation has error over [−q,0), mean −q/2, and variance q²/12, so it introduces DC bias. Rounding has error bounded by ±q/2, zero ideal mean, and variance q²/12; round-to-even removes the slight upward tie bias of ordinary round-to-nearest. [§§12.3.3–12.3.4, Eqs. 12-23–12-26, Figs. 12-7–12-9]
Preserve full precision through a chain of arithmetic and round or truncate only once, at the final operation, to minimize accumulated quantization error. [§12.3.4]

A floating-point value is n=m·2^e, with word bits divided between exponent range and mantissa precision. Normalization places the leading one at a known location, allowing formats such as IEEE P754 to omit it as a hidden bit. [§12.4, Eqs. 12-27–12-34, Table 12-6]

Block floating point normalizes a whole array to one shared exponent, then performs fixed-point arithmetic; when a stage overflows, all words shift right and the shared exponent increments. It extends fixed-point range with less hardware than full floating point, but cannot match full floating-point performance. [§12.5]

Changing the sign of alternating samples, multiplication by (−1)^n, translates a spectrum by fs/2; the repeating {1,0,−1,0} and {0,−1,0,1} sequences perform quadrature translation by −fs/4 using routing and sign changes rather than general multipliers (Sec. 13.1, PDF pp. 589–593).

For real fs/4-centered input, combining the sparse mixer outputs with alternating FIR coefficients and decimation by two halves the multiplication workload; a half-band filter collapses the quadrature branch to delays plus one center-coefficient operation (Sec. 13.1.3, PDF pp. 593–595).

The alpha-Max-plus-beta-Min family estimates sqrt(I^2+Q^2) with a comparison, scaled Max/Min terms, and an add; power-of-two coefficient choices turn scaling into shifts, while the more accurate piecewise form cited in Eq. 13-7′ stays within about one percent (Sec. 13.2, PDF pp. 596–598).

A generalized cosine window has only three relevant spectral terms, so a windowed FFT bin can be formed from the unwindowed bin and its two neighbors; Hanning coefficients further reduce the operation to shifts and additions (Sec. 13.3, PDF pp. 599–601).

Packing two real sequences into the real and imaginary parts of one complex FFT permits recovery of both real FFTs, and packing even/odd samples of a 2N-point real sequence permits recovery from one N-point complex FFT (Sec. 13.5, PDF pp. 603–612).

An inverse DFT can be implemented with a forward FFT either by conjugating input and output with 1/N scaling, or by swapping real and imaginary parts before and after the forward transform and applying the same scaling (Sec. 13.6, PDF pp. 613–614).
A symmetric S-tap linear-phase FIR needs only (S+1)/2 multiplications for odd S or S/2 for even S when mirror samples are pre-added in a folded realization (Sec. 13.7, PDF pp. 615–616).

Ideal quantization-noise power is lsb^2/12 and its flat PSD scales inversely with sample rate; oversampling improves quantization SNR by 10 log10(fs,new/fs,old) dB, so a factor of four yields 6.02 dB, approximately one extra bit (Sec. 13.8.1, PDF pp. 617–618).

Dither trades a higher broadband noise floor for decorrelated quantization error and lower coherent spurs; the text recommends roughly 1/3–1 lsb RMS for ordinary wideband dither and explains triangular and subtractive variants (Sec. 13.8.2, PDF pp. 618–620).

Coherent A/D testing uses an input tone at mfs/N to eliminate FFT leakage; odd-prime m exercises more converter codes, SINAD is total signal-bin power divided by all remaining positive-frequency noise/distortion power, and missing codes appear as zero-count histogram bins (Sec. 13.9, PDF pp. 621–626).

For sequences of lengths P and Q, FFT convolution requires transform size N at least P+Q−1; long streams use overlap-save or overlap-add, and the stored filter spectrum is computed only once (Sec. 13.10, PDF pp. 627–631).

Summing M independent uniform random variables approaches a normal distribution; the sum has mean M/2 and variance M/12, after which shifting and scaling sets an arbitrary target mean and standard deviation (Sec. 13.11, PDF pp. 632–633).

Forward filtering, straight reversal, filtering again with the same IIR filter, and final reversal cancels filter phase offline; the composite magnitude response is squared, so passband ripple and stopband attenuation in dB both double (Sec. 13.12, PDF pp. 634–635).

Filter sharpening combines delayed and cascaded copies of an existing integer-group-delay FIR response to reduce both stopband leakage and passband ripple without changing its coefficients; the cited low-order scheme can make b-bit coefficients behave roughly like b+4-bit coefficients (Sec. 13.13, PDF pp. 635–637).

A Goertzel resonator computes one N-point DFT bin with N+2 real multiplications and 2N+1 additions for real input, needs no power-of-two N or input-block storage, and is multiplication-cheaper than an FFT for M requested tones when M < log2(N) (Sec. 13.17, PDF pp. 644–647).

The single-bin sliding DFT update subtracts the sample leaving the N-point window, adds the new sample, and rotates the result, requiring two real additions and one complex multiply per new output independent of N (Sec. 13.18.1, PDF pp. 648–651).

A unit-circle SDFT pole is only marginally stable; moving the pole and comb zeros to radius r<1 guarantees stability but perturbs exact DFT equivalence. Adjacent-bin frequency-domain convolution supplies Hamming/Hanning leakage reduction without time-domain window multiplications (Secs. 13.18.2–13.18.3, PDF pp. 651–654).

Changing the SDFT comb coefficient from −1 to +1 rotates all comb zeros by pi/N, allowing analyzer centers at either 2pi m/N or 2pi(m+1/2)/N and hence 2N selectable frequencies (Sec. 13.18.4, PDF p. 654).

A Zoom FFT gains narrowband resolution by complex down-conversion, lowpass filtering, decimation by D, and an N/D-point FFT; increased D reduces FFT work but demands a narrower, more expensive anti-alias filter (Sec. 13.19, PDF pp. 654–657).

A real-time DC-removal filter places a zero at z=1 and a pole at z=alpha; alpha nearer one narrows the DC notch, while error-feedback quantization shapes truncation noise away from DC in fixed-point implementations (Sec. 13.23, PDF pp. 664–667).

Horner's rule reduces a kth-order polynomial to k multiply-add stages; Estrin's regrouping preserves the arithmetic count but exposes independent MAC operations for parallel hardware (Sec. 13.26, PDF pp. 673–675).

A very high-order FIR can be designed from a shorter prototype by DFT-domain zero insertion and a longer inverse DFT; cutoff frequencies in the prototype are expanded by interpolation factor M, and the final impulse response is scaled by M (Sec. 13.27, PDF pp. 675–678).

Exact FFT-based interpolation of a real sequence must split a nonzero Nyquist-bin sample equally between the two conjugate-symmetric locations after zero insertion; the source spectrum must have negligible energy near ±fs/2 to avoid endpoint errors (Sec. 13.28.1, PDF pp. 678–679).

For independent noise blocks, averaging N realizations divides variance by N and standard deviation by sqrt(N); biased variance uses 1/N while Bessel-corrected unbiased variance uses 1/(N−1), with about one-percent difference at N=100 (Appendix D.2–D.3, PDF pp. 757–760).

Variance can be computed in one pass from accumulated x(n) and x(n)^2 terms, saving about N additions and eliminating storage of all N past samples; recursive running sums extend this identity to sliding real-time averages and variances (Secs. 13.35–13.36, PDF pp. 694–699).

Filter group delay can be obtained without arctangents or phase unwrapping from the real part of the ratio DFT[kh(k)]/DFT[h(k)], with zero-padding used to refine frequency granularity and explicit handling required at response zeros (Sec. 13.48, PDF pp. 722–724).

Replacing every unit delay in a quantized 2nd-order lowpass IIR section by M delays moves each pole from re^(±jtheta) to radius r^(1/M) and angle ±theta/M; a following multiplier-free CIC rejects images, yielding a narrowband interpolated-IIR without wider coefficients or extra IIR multiplies (Sec. 13.50, PDF pp. 725–729).

A stable Goertzel variant heterodynes the target bin to DC, sums the N translated samples with an exactly representable DC resonator, and uses the chapter's guaranteed-stable quadrature oscillator to prevent mixer-amplitude drift (Sec. 13.51, PDF pp. 729–731).

For a real N-point sequence, circular time reversal conjugates its DFT; straight reversal adds the corresponding linear-phase factor because it is a shifted circular reversal (Appendix C, PDF pp. 751–754).

Relative power ratios use 10log10(P2/P1) dB, amplitude ratios use 20log10(A2/A1) when impedance is fixed, and dBm is an absolute level referenced to one milliwatt rather than a relative dB value (Appendix E, PDF pp. 770–777).

Appendix I gives constructive DFT-based algorithms for symmetric Chebyshev windows used in FIR design and nonsymmetric Chebyshev windows used in spectral analysis; sidelobe target −20gamma dB sets the control parameter (PDF pp. 808–811).
pedagogy: Lyons teaches DSP as an engineer-facing, intuition-first discipline: sampled plots, spectra, block diagrams, pole-zero geometry, and small numerical examples usually establish the behavior before concise algebraic derivations formalize it. Proofs are constructive and informal—by substitution, transform identities, symmetry, or inspection—while implementation consequences remain central: sign and scaling conventions, aliasing, group delay, coefficient precision, accumulator growth, stability, memory traffic, multiply/add counts, and cases where an elegant architecture loses its advantage. Chapters 1–12 build a broadly linear foundation from sequences and sampling through transforms, FIR/IIR design, specialized filters, quadrature/Hilbert methods, multirate processing, averaging, and finite-word formats; Chapter 13 then becomes a practicing-engineer’s cookbook of 51 reusable tricks in no prescribed order, and Appendices A–I supply prerequisite refreshers plus dense derivations and design tables. Worked examples use explicit data, sample rates, attenuation and transition targets, tap counts, hardware limits, and deliberately misleading or broken constructions that learners must diagnose. The substantial Chapters 1–12 problem sets mix conceptual explanations, sketches, hand calculations, derivations, block-diagram transformations, coefficient design, software plots, vendor-device scenarios, and lab-ready multi-part tasks; Chapter 13 has no conventional problem set but repeatedly invites verification, modeling, architecture comparison, coefficient-quantization experiments, and empirical tuning. Expected prerequisites are algebra, trigonometry, complex numbers, basic calculus, introductory probability/statistics, discrete sequences, convolution, and elementary systems concepts; transforms are motivated in the book, though Chapter 13 assumes working fluency with DFT/FFT, z-transforms, FIR/IIR structures, multirate systems, and fixed-point arithmetic. A strong reuse pattern is: predict from a diagram, calculate a small case, inspect a spectrum or pole plot, implement it, then confront the numerical or architectural pitfall.

gems: Sec. 1.1 (PDF p. 27): the insistence that there is literally no defined signal between plotted samples is a small but powerful correction to the common habit of mentally connecting the dots.
Sec. 1.8 (PDF pp. 42-43): a four-point moving average is introduced by striking the system with a unit impulse, then reading both the coefficient sequence and lowpass behavior from the response.
Sec. 2.1 (PDF pp. 52-55): the 7 kHz versus 1 kHz alias produced at a 6 kHz sample rate makes frequency ambiguity immediately audible/visual rather than merely algebraic.
Sec. 2.3 (PDF pp. 59-63): a band centered near 20 MHz with only 5 MHz bandwidth can occupy valid sampling intervals around 11.25-11.67 MHz instead of forcing a conventional rate above 45 MHz.
Sec. 2.4 (PDF pp. 63-65): the 'shark's teeth' view of successive spectral zones makes alternating normal/inverted aliases memorable, and (-1)^n becomes a one-multiply-per-sample repair.
Sec. 3.1 (PDF pp. 75-85): the hand-worked 8-point DFT of 1 kHz and 2 kHz sinusoids sampled at 8 kHz is compact enough for learners to verify every real and imaginary contribution.

Secs. 3.8-3.9 (PDF pp. 92-106): keeping the record length fixed while changing a tone from 3.0 to 3.4 cycles, then adding a weak second tone and windowing, provides a complete leakage-to-detection narrative.
Sec. 3.11 (PDF pp. 107-110): padding the same 16 samples to successively larger transforms visually separates 'more dots on the same curve' from genuine resolving power.
Sec. 3.12 (PDF pp. 110-113): one repeated tone-in-noise example at three N values turns the abstract 3 dB-per-doubling processing gain into an obvious measurement advantage.
Sec. 4.1 (PDF pp. 138-140): the scale comparison is vivid: a 2,097,152-point FFT is framed as seconds of work while the direct DFT would require weeks on the same basis.
Sec. 4.2 (PDF pp. 140-143): the practical ordering rule 'subtract the mean, window the acquired samples, then append zeros' prevents several common spectral-analysis mistakes in one line of workflow.
Secs. 5.1-5.2 (PDF pp. 168-181): a five-minute moving average of bridge traffic is an unusually accessible bridge from an everyday table to convolution, impulse response, and lowpass filtering.

Sec. 5.6 (PDF pp. 197-200): the historical aside about Parks and McClellan's exchange-method paper being rejected is paired with the Beatles/Decca rejection, making algorithmic novelty and peer-review fallibility memorable.
Sec. 5.7 (PDF pp. 200-201): the 31-tap half-band example collapses to 17 multiplies because of alternating zeros and symmetry, a strong structure-before-optimization lesson.
Sec. 5.8 (PDF pp. 201-206): the group-delay discussion ties a straight phase line directly to preserving a signal's component alignment instead of treating linear phase as a cosmetic plot property.

Sec. 6.4.2 (PDF pp. 258-262): the mnemonic 'z-domain produces less pain' accompanies a real modeling advantage: writing equations from z^-1 block notation usually introduces fewer intermediate unknowns.
Sec. 6.6.1 (PDF pp. 267-269): Lyons sharply distinguishes recursive/nonrecursive as implementation structure from IIR/FIR as impulse-response duration, correcting a widespread terminology shortcut.

Sec. 6.7 (PDF pp. 270-272): an integer-rounded, zero-input second-order filter that rings forever is a laboratory-ready demonstration that mathematical stability does not guarantee a quiet fixed-point implementation.
Sec. 6.8.2 (PDF pp. 274-276): 'biquad' is motivated both by the two quadratic polynomials and, humorously, because the word sounds cool; the levity helps anchor a central implementation unit.
Sec. 6.10 (PDF pp. 288-292): the warning that any spectrum or filter response nonzero at +fs/2 should trigger immediate aliasing suspicion is a concise review heuristic.

Sec. 6.13 (PDF pp. 303-305): the recommendation to code and time both candidates when choosing IIR versus FIR exposes why multiplier counts alone can mislead on DSP hardware with zero-overhead MAC loops.
A nine-sample matched-filter template is hidden twice in strong random noise; the output correlation peaks recover both events and make threshold tradeoffs concrete. [§7.3.2, Figs. 7-12–7-13]
IFIR design example: a conventional 137-tap lowpass becomes 45 model taps plus 25 image-reject taps—70 total, about a 49% reduction. [§7.4.5]

A more demanding IFIR example (f_pass=0.02f_s, transition 0.01f_s, 50 dB) uses M=7 and 33+27=60 taps instead of roughly 240, a 75% reduction; the text notes savings can approach 90% for under 10% extra memory. [§7.4.5]

The six-section N=62 Type-IV FSF example meets 0.05f_s cutoff, 0.095f_s stopband start, ≤0.3 dB ripple, and ≥65 dB attenuation with 17 multiplies and 19 adds, versus 30 multiplies and 59 adds for a folded 60-tap Parks–McClellan FIR. [§7.5.12, Figs. 7-46–7-47]
The warning that theory and practice differ because in theory they do not is deployed exactly where finite precision threatens nominally perfect FSF pole-zero cancellation. [§7.5.3]

A complexity-only comparison is likened to modern swimwear: what it shows matters, and what it omits is vital—an invitation to include memory, control, and numeric behavior alongside multiply counts. [§7.5.11, Fig. 7-45]

Euler’s identity is called the Rosetta Stone of quadrature signal processing, then made physical as a corkscrew trajectory whose projections are cosine and sine and whose XY oscilloscope trace is a circle. [§8.3, Figs. 8-5–8-8]

A 50 MHz band can be bandpass-sampled at 40 MHz and shifted digitally by f_s/4=10 MHz; the I/Q local-oscillator sequences are only 1, 0, −1, 0 and 0, −1, 0, 1, eliminating general multipliers. [§8.9, Figs. 8-22–8-24]

The analytic signal shifts a 25 kHz real signal cleanly to 20 kHz by multiplication with exp(−j2π·5000t), avoiding the difficult image-rejection filter that a real mixer would require. [§9.2, Fig. 9-8]

The 400 kHz-to-4 kHz decimator with a 0–1.8 kHz retained band and 60 dB rejection is estimated at 2727 taps as one stage; factoring 100 as 25×4 cuts the design to a few hundred taps. [§10.2.2, Fig. 10-4]
CIC filters are described as ‘lean, mean, fat-free filtering machines’: add/subtract-only structures that turn a severe multirate task into low-rate comb work plus high-rate accumulators. [§10.14]

The CIC two’s-complement example makes intentional overflow tangible: an integrator can wrap repeatedly, yet modulo arithmetic lets the downstream comb recover the correct result when word width meets the output bound. [§10.14.4, Fig. 10-40]
A pulse of amplitude 2.5 is visually lost in one noisy record, begins to emerge after 32 coherent averages, and is unmistakable after 256. [§11.1, Figs. 11-1–11-3]

The chapter punctures a common misconception: averaging 10 or 100 FFT magnitudes makes the spectrum steadier but does not improve the actual signal-to-noise ratio or lower the mean noise floor. [§11.2, Fig. 11-4]
A charge-card magnetic-stripe reader motivates exponential averaging as a practical compromise between smoothing and the need to respond before the card has already passed the sensor. [§11.6.3]

The dynamic exponential averager starts with a large α for fast acquisition and decreases it over time for quiet steady-state estimates, turning an apparent smoothing-versus-response tradeoff into a scheduling problem. [§11.6.3]

The 64-bit counter aside notes that incrementing once per second since the beginning of the universe would still leave its four most significant bits zero—a memorable scale for 2^64. [§12.2, footnote to Eq. 12-6]
The 8-bit A/D example turns one LSB into 7.81 mV over a ±1 V range, then follows the resulting ±3.905 mV error from a time-domain staircase into broadband DFT noise. [§12.3.1, Figs. 12-1–12-2]

A full-scale ideal 8-bit converter reaches only 49.9 dB SNR, so digitizing a 55 dB analog signal loses information; a 10-bit ideal converter’s roughly 62 dB ceiling is the safer match. [§12.3.1, discussion after Eq. 12-15]

The overflow section escalates from an eight-digit calculator turning 99,999,999+1 into 1 to an FFT butterfly whose real or imaginary component can more than double in one stage. [§12.3.2, Eqs. 12-17–12-21]
Dividing 31 by 16 via a four-bit right shift returns 1 instead of 1.9375—roughly 50% error—making truncation’s dependence on discarded bits and residual magnitude painfully concrete. [§12.3.3]
Block floating point is presented as a marriage: an FFT block shares one exponent, behaves like fixed point until overflow, then shifts every word and increments the shared exponent. [§12.5]

A three-valued fs/4 oscillator uses only 1, 0, and −1, turning complex down-conversion into sign changes and routing; with a half-band filter, the quadrature path can collapse to delays plus a shift (Sec. 13.1, PDF pp. 591–595).

The simple Max+0.5Min magnitude estimate overshoots a unit vector by 11.8 percent near 26 degrees, making a memorable motivation for the better alpha/beta coefficient pairs (Sec. 13.2, PDF pp. 596–598).

Oversampling a converter from 100 kHz to 400 kHz gives 10log10(4)=6.02 dB improvement—one extra effective bit obtained with speed and filtering rather than a more expensive ADC (Sec. 13.8.1, PDF p. 618).
In the 5-bit coherent-sampling example, the clean m=5 record measures SINAD 31.6 dB, essentially the ideal 31.7 dB; deliberately dropped bits collapse it to 15.2 dB (Sec. 13.9.1, PDF pp. 622–625).

Fast convolution is presented with a practical crossover rather than dogma: an FFT implementation often wins only when the FIR impulse response reaches roughly 40–80 taps, depending on hardware and software (Sec. 13.10, PDF pp. 627–631).

The single-tone example seeks 30 kHz at fs=128 kHz with a 64-point FFT: computing all bins to keep X(15) throws away 98 percent of the computed outputs, a crisp motivation for Goertzel (Sec. 13.17, PDF pp. 644–647).

After its initial N-sample fill, the SDFT updates one exact DFT bin for each new sample with only two real additions and one complex multiply, independent of transform length (Sec. 13.18, PDF pp. 648–651).

A tuned three-tap linear-phase FIR with one non-unity coefficient removes 4.1-kHz narrowband interference by about 54 dB using only two additions and one multiply per output (Sec. 13.34, PDF pp. 690–692).

A prototype with 168 taps is expanded by ten in the frequency domain to create a usable 1680-tap linear-phase FIR after high-order Remez software is said to become unreliable above roughly 400–500 taps (Sec. 13.27, PDF pp. 675–678).

Filter sharpening is framed as a hardware rescue: an immutable 8-bit-coefficient FIR can achieve roughly 12-bit-coefficient response quality by recombining delayed and cascaded copies (Sec. 13.13, PDF pp. 635–637).

The impulsive-noise worked block {10,10,11,9,10,10,13,10,10,10} has ordinary mean 10.3 but corrected mean 10.096 after trimming and imbalance correction, demonstrating resistance to spikes (Sec. 13.25, PDF pp. 671–673).

Appendix A's four-bit example shows that rectangular storage can represent 7+j7 while polar storage with magnitude limited to 7 overflows—the same complex number can fit or fail solely because of representation (Appendix A.4, PDF pp. 745–746).
Appendix C turns six samples into points on a circle to show why circular reversal and ordinary left-right reversal are not the same discrete operation (Appendix C, PDF pp. 751–753).

The statistics appendix uses the two-child puzzle to force normalization over all outcomes, giving one-third—not one-half—for a known daughter having a sister under the source's stated sample space (Appendix D.6, PDF pp. 765–766).

The normal-distribution reference marks 68.27 percent of values within one standard deviation and 99.73 percent within three, tying visual probability mass directly to DSP noise tests (Appendix D.7, PDF pp. 767–768).
The Chebyshev-window construction works a complete N=9, 60-dB-sidelobe example and then shows the related even-length nonsymmetric window used for spectrum analysis (Appendix I, PDF pp. 808–811).
chapter_map: Front matter (PDF pp. 1-25): establishes the book's practical-engineer audience, notation, learning posture, and detailed route through the assigned chapters.

Chapter 1, Discrete Sequences and Systems (PDF pp. 26-51): builds the sampled-sequence vocabulary, block-diagram primitives, LTI tests, impulse response, convolution, and frequency response; use as the conceptual entry module.

Chapter 2, Periodic Sampling (PDF pp. 52-73): develops aliasing from sinusoidal ambiguity through lowpass and bandpass sampling, spectral inversion, and noise folding; use before any acquisition or resampling lab.

Chapter 3, The Discrete Fourier Transform (PDF pp. 74-137): interprets every DFT term, then develops symmetry, scaling, shifts, leakage, windows, scalloping, resolution, zero padding, processing gain, rectangular transforms, and DTFT context; this is the core spectral-analysis module.

Chapter 5, Finite Impulse Response Filters (PDF pp. 167-236): introduces convolutional filtering, develops window and Parks-McClellan design, modulation, half-band efficiency, linear phase/group delay, generic convolution, and response analysis; use as the primary FIR design-and-implementation module.

Chapter 6, Infinite Impulse Response Filters (PDF pp. 237-327): develops Laplace/z-plane intuition, poles/zeros, structures, fixed-point failure modes, cascaded biquads, scaling, impulse-invariance, bilinear, and optimized design, ending with an evidence-based FIR/IIR choice; use as a combined IIR theory, implementation, and design module.
